intro: Welcome! In this lesson you train your ears: you'll catch letters, numbers and names when people speak slowly, and understand greetings and simple classroom instructions. You don't need every word — listen for the key words. Warm-up: what do you say when a teacher says 'Good morning, class!'?
teachingNotes: This is a listening lesson: most practice is 'press play, then answer'. Encourage learners to listen for key words (a name, a number, an action like open or close) rather than every word, and to replay as often as they need.
Letter names Indonesian ears confuse: E ('ee') vs I ('eye'), G ('jee') vs J ('jay'), A ('ay') vs R ('ar'), plus W ('double-you'), Y ('why') and H ('aitch'). 'Double N' means NN.

Phone numbers are said digit by digit in small groups; 0 is often 'oh', and 55 can be 'double five'. The classic trap is thirteen (stress at the end) vs thirty (stress at the start). Prices: 'twenty-five thousand rupiah' — thousand, with no s.

Greetings: Good morning / afternoon / evening when you meet someone; Good night only when leaving or going to bed (a common Indonesian error is 'Good night' on arrival). The reply to How are you? is I'm fine, thanks. And you?

Classroom instructions are short commands: Listen. Repeat. Open / Close your book. Sit down. Stand up. Write your name. Look at the board. Learners only need to understand and act — don't teach the imperative as grammar, and use no new tenses.
Z is 'zed' in British English and 'zee' in American English; the audio voice may use either, so accept both and say so.

Explain 'stress' in plain words the first time (the part of the word said louder and longer). 'oh' for 0 is because 0 looks like the letter O. After a number, thousand never takes -s (twenty thousand), even though it's many thousands.
p.m. = after midday (6 p.m. = 18.00), a.m. = before midday; learners use the 24-hour clock in writing.

keyPoints.title: Letters, numbers and names
keyPoints.explanation: Names are spelled with English letter names, which are different from Indonesian ones (E is 'ee', I is 'eye'), so listen for the pairs that sound alike (E/I, G/J, A/R). Phone numbers come digit by digit, with 'oh' for 0 and 'double' for two of the same. For 13–19 the stress (the louder, longer part) is at the end; for 30, 40, 50… it is at the start.

id.title: Huruf, angka, dan nama
id.explanation: Nama dieja dengan nama huruf bahasa Inggris, yang berbeda dari bahasa Indonesia (E dibaca 'ii', I dibaca 'ai'), jadi hati-hati dengan pasangan yang bunyinya mirip (E/I, G/J, A/R). Nomor telepon disebut satu per satu angkanya, dengan 'oh' untuk 0 dan 'double' untuk dua angka yang sama. Untuk 13–19, tekanan (bagian yang lebih keras dan panjang) ada di akhir; untuk 30, 40, 50… tekanannya di awal.

keyPoints.title: Greetings and classroom instructions
keyPoints.explanation: Greetings change with the time of day; Good night is only for leaving. Classroom instructions start with the action word: open, close, sit, stand, write, look, listen, repeat.

id.title: Salam dan instruksi di kelas
id.explanation: Salam berubah sesuai waktu: pagi, siang, sore, malam. Good night hanya untuk pamit. Instruksi di kelas diawali kata tindakan: open, close, sit, stand, write, look, listen, repeat.

blocks.text: When you listen, you **don't need every word**. Listen for the **key words**: a name, a number, a greeting, or an action like *open* or *sit*. Playing the audio again is normal. In real life you can say: **Sorry? Can you repeat that, please?** or **Slowly, please.**

id.text: Saat menyimak, kamu **tidak perlu menangkap setiap kata**. Dengarkan **kata kuncinya**: nama, angka, salam, atau tindakan seperti *open* atau *sit*. Memutar ulang audio itu wajar. Dalam kehidupan nyata kamu bisa bilang: **Sorry? Can you repeat that, please?** atau **Slowly, please.**

blocks.text: Listen once for the general idea, then again for the detail you need — the number, the name, the action.

id.text: Dengarkan sekali untuk gambaran umumnya, lalu sekali lagi untuk detail yang kamu perlukan — angkanya, namanya, tindakannya.

blocks.prompt: You hear: 'Please open your book at page ten.' What are the key words?
blocks.explain: Open (the action), book (the thing) and ten (the page) tell you what to do. Please and your are small helper words.

id.explain: Open (tindakan), book (bendanya) dan ten (halamannya) memberitahu apa yang harus dilakukan. Please dan your hanya kata bantu kecil.
id.prompt: Kamu mendengar: 'Please open your book at page ten.' Mana kata kuncinya?

blocks.text: People spell names letter by letter with the **English letter names**. They are not the same as Indonesian letter names: in Indonesian, E is said 'e' and I is said 'i', but in English **E** is 'ee' and **I** is 'eye'. Listen carefully for the pairs that sound alike to Indonesian ears: **E** ('ee') and **I** ('eye'), **G** ('jee') and **J** ('jay'), **A** ('ay') and **R** ('ar'). **Double** means two of the same letter.

id.text: Orang mengeja nama huruf demi huruf dengan **nama huruf versi Inggris**. Nama huruf ini tidak sama dengan bahasa Indonesia: kita membaca E 'e' dan I 'i', tapi dalam bahasa Inggris **E** dibaca 'ii' (i panjang) dan **I** dibaca 'ai'. Dengarkan baik-baik pasangan yang terdengar mirip bagi telinga Indonesia: **E** ('ee', dibaca ii) dan **I** ('eye', dibaca ai), **G** ('jee', dibaca ji) dan **J** ('jay', dibaca jei), **A** ('ay', dibaca ei) dan **R** ('ar'). **Double** berarti dua huruf yang sama.

rows.id: W dibaca 'dabel-yu' (bentuknya seperti dua U), Y dibaca 'wai'.

blocks.text: The trap: English **E** sounds like Indonesian *i*, and English **I** sounds like *ai*. When you hear 'ee', write **E**; when you hear 'eye', write **I**. And **Z** has two names: British English says 'zed', American English says 'zee'. Both mean Z.

id.text: Jebakannya: **E** bahasa Inggris terdengar seperti *i* bahasa Indonesia, dan **I** terdengar seperti *ai*. Kalau kamu dengar 'ii', tulis **E**; kalau dengar 'ai', tulis **I**. Lalu **Z** punya dua nama: bahasa Inggris British bilang 'zed', bahasa Inggris Amerika bilang 'zi'. Dua-duanya artinya Z.

blocks.prompt: You hear: 'jay, oh, kay, oh'. Which name is it?
blocks.explain: 'Jay' is J and 'kay' is K, so it's J-O-K-O: Joko. G is 'jee', and 'oh' is the letter O.

id.explain: 'Jay' adalah J dan 'kay' adalah K, jadi J-O-K-O: Joko. G dibaca 'jee', dan 'oh' adalah huruf O.
id.prompt: Kamu mendengar: 'jay, oh, kay, oh'. Nama yang mana?

blocks.text:
**Phone numbers** are said one digit at a time, in small groups: *oh-eight-one-two*. People often say **oh** for 0 (because 0 looks like the letter O) and **double** for two of the same digit (*double five* = 55).

For **13–19** the **stress** is at the end (thir**TEEN**); for **30, 40, 50…** it is at the start (**THIR**ty). **Stress** means the part of the word that is said **louder and longer**; here it's written in capitals.

Prices: *twenty thousand rupiah* = Rp20.000. After a number, **thousand** has **no -s**, even though it's many thousands: *twenty thousand*, not 'twenty thousands'.

id.text:
**Nomor telepon** diucapkan satu angka demi satu angka, dalam kelompok kecil: *oh-eight-one-two*. Orang sering bilang **oh** untuk 0 (karena 0 bentuknya seperti huruf O) dan **double** untuk dua angka yang sama (*double five* = 55).

Untuk **13–19** **tekanannya** di akhir (thir**TEEN**); untuk **30, 40, 50…** tekanannya di awal (**THIR**ty). **Tekanan** artinya bagian kata yang diucapkan **lebih keras dan lebih panjang**; di sini ditulis dengan huruf besar.

Harga: *twenty thousand rupiah* = Rp20.000. Setelah angka, **thousand** **tidak** pakai -s, walaupun jumlahnya ribuan: *twenty thousand*, bukan 'twenty thousands'.

id.note: dengarkan bagian yang ditekan (diucapkan lebih keras)

blocks.text: Not sure? Check politely: *Thirteen — one, three?* People are happy to confirm.

id.text: Tidak yakin? Pastikan dengan sopan: *Thirteen — one, three?* Orang senang mengonfirmasi.

blocks.prompt: You hear 'SIX-ty', with the stress at the start. Which number is it?
blocks.explain: Stress at the start means a -ty number: SIXty = 60. Sixteen has the stress at the end: sixTEEN.

id.explain: Tekanan di awal berarti angka -ty: SIXty = 60. Sixteen tekanannya di akhir: sixTEEN.
id.prompt: Kamu mendengar 'SIX-ty', dengan tekanan di awal. Angka berapa itu?

blocks.text: Greetings change with the time of day: **Good morning** (until about 12), **Good afternoon** (12–6 p.m.), **Good evening** (after 6 p.m.). **p.m.** means after midday, so 6 p.m. = 18.00; **a.m.** means before midday. **Good night** is not hello — it means goodbye at night or before bed. When someone asks **How are you?**, answer **I'm fine, thanks. And you?**

id.text: Salam berubah sesuai waktu: **Good morning** (sampai sekitar jam 12), **Good afternoon** (jam 12–18), **Good evening** (setelah jam 18). **p.m.** artinya setelah tengah hari, jadi 6 p.m. = jam 18.00; **a.m.** artinya sebelum tengah hari. **Good night** bukan salam bertemu — artinya selamat tinggal di malam hari atau sebelum tidur. Kalau seseorang bertanya **How are you?**, jawab **I'm fine, thanks. And you?**

rows.note: reply: Nice to meet you too.

id.note: balasannya: Nice to meet you too.

blocks.text: Indonesian 'selamat malam' has two English versions: **Good evening** when you arrive, **Good night** when you leave.

id.text: 'Selamat malam' punya dua versi dalam bahasa Inggris: **Good evening** saat datang, **Good night** saat pamit.

blocks.prompt: It's 8 p.m. You arrive at a party and the host says hello. What does she say?
blocks.explain: 8 p.m. is in the evening (20.00). After 6 p.m., hello is Good evening. Good night is only for leaving or going to bed.

id.explain: 8 p.m. = jam 8 malam (20.00). Setelah jam 18, salam bertemu adalah Good evening. Good night hanya untuk pamit atau mau tidur.
id.prompt: Sekarang jam 8 malam (8 p.m.). Kamu datang ke sebuah pesta dan tuan rumah menyapamu. Apa yang dia ucapkan?

blocks.text: Teachers give short instructions that start with the **action word**: *Listen. Repeat. Open your book. Close your book. Sit down. Stand up. Write your name. Look at the board.* Catch the first word and you know what to do. Often you'll also hear **please**, at the start or at the end: it's like *tolong* or *silakan* and makes the instruction polite.

id.text: Guru memberi instruksi pendek yang diawali **kata tindakan**: *Listen. Repeat. Open your book. Close your book. Sit down. Stand up. Write your name. Look at the board.* Tangkap kata pertamanya dan kamu tahu apa yang harus dilakukan. Sering juga ada kata **please**, di awal atau di akhir: artinya seperti *tolong* atau *silakan*, supaya instruksinya sopan.

blocks.text: Open ↔ close and sit down ↔ stand up are opposites. Listen carefully to the first word: it changes everything.

id.text: Open ↔ close dan sit down ↔ stand up saling berlawanan. Dengarkan baik-baik kata pertamanya: itu mengubah segalanya.

blocks.prompt: The teacher says 'Look at the board.' Where do you look?
blocks.explain: Board = papan tulis, so you look at the board.

id.explain: Board = papan tulis, jadi kamu melihat ke papan tulis.
id.prompt: Guru berkata 'Look at the board.' Kamu melihat ke mana?

What does 'double' mean when someone spells a name?
When do I say good evening and when good night?
What can I say when I don't understand?

id.intro: Selamat datang! Di pelajaran ini kamu melatih telingamu: menangkap huruf, angka dan nama saat orang berbicara pelan, serta memahami salam dan instruksi sederhana di kelas. Kamu tidak perlu menangkap setiap kata — dengarkan kata kuncinya. Pemanasan: apa jawabanmu kalau guru bilang 'Good morning, class!'?
suggestedQuestions: Bagaimana cara mendengar beda thirteen dan thirty?
Apa arti 'double' saat seseorang mengeja nama?
Kapan bilang good evening dan kapan good night?
Apa yang bisa aku katakan kalau tidak mengerti?
